clue.text: Bill praises mum for bringing in gifts

indicators.note: one word bringing in another takes it inside itself, between its own letters

blocks.note: AC, short for account, is a bill
a plural noun: words of praise
mum means silent, and SH is the call for silence

explanation.surface: A bill full of flattery for mother, in exchange for some presents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' looks like a mother but means 'quiet!', the sense in 'keep mum'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gifts in the sense of talents or skills are a person's accomplishments, the things they can do well.

clue.text: Where to find her Simon at night, perhaps?

definitions.note: a question word standing for a place, here an English county

indicators.note: perhaps says the words before it are only one possible arrangement, so their letters may be put in another order

blocks.note: fifteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about where a woman's partner Simon spends his evenings.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole of 'her Simon at night' is the fodder, all fifteen letters; Nottinghamshire is an English county in the East Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a place, an English county, so it answers a question asking where.

clue.text: MB, sure rise can be arranged, makes repayment

indicators.note: things that can be arranged can be put into a different order, as these letters are

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A financial deal: an MB qualification and a guaranteed pay rise can be fixed up in return for paying money back.
explanation.definitionFit: To reimburse someone is to pay back money they have spent, so it means repaying them.

clue.text: Germ-free month I take into account

indicators.note: to take something into an account is to place it inside, so the first pieces go within the last

blocks.note: AC is the usual abbreviation for account
SEPT is the short form of September
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone books a month into their accounts, as a bookkeeping entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Aseptic describes surgical conditions with no bacteria or other microbes present, which is what free of germs means.

clue.text: Risk having airmen standing around back of plane

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing up means reading from the bottom upwards, so the word runs backwards
around says the airmen surround the other letter
the back of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: the RAF is the Royal Air Force, Britain's airmen
the final letter of plane

explanation.surface: A daring pilot takes a chance, with crew gathered round the tail of the aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: Fear can mean a chance or likelihood of something bad, as in 'no fear of that', the same as a risk.

clue.text: Cold individual dropping in in a snooty way

indicators.note: the second in says the word for dropping goes inside the word for individual

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
only as in an only child, a single individual one
going down

explanation.surface: A frosty person drops in on others with an air of superiority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dropping in' reads as paying a visit, but the 'in' is a container signal; the individual is an only one.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting condescendingly is behaving as if superior to others, which is what a snooty manner shows.

clue.text: Sad fact is it is no different, which leads to complaints

indicators.note: the letters are to be made different, put into a new order

blocks.clueFragment: Sad fact is it is no
blocks.note: fifteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A gloomy observation that nothing changes, which is why people grumble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No different' reads as a phrase, but 'no' belongs to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Dissatisfaction is the feeling of being unhappy with something, and it is what prompts people to complain.

clue.text: Second company store ordered small motor-cycles

indicators.note: a store put in order has been sorted afresh, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
CO is the abbreviation for company
fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: A second firm's shop has placed an order for little motorbikes.
explanation.definitionFit: Motor scooters are light motorised two-wheelers with small wheels and a step-through frame.

clue.text: Blue with cold, I rushed back

indicators.note: going back means the letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for cold
taken as written
tore as in tore along, moved at speed

explanation.surface: Someone turned blue with cold and hurried home again.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue here is not a colour but means risqué, as in a blue film.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue in the sense of sexually explicit or smutty material is a common British synonym for erotic.

clue.text: Water bed?

blocks.note: surface reading: a waterbed, a mattress filled with water
setter's reading: the bed of a body of water, such as a river or sea, its lowest part

explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like the furniture, but read separately they mean the floor beneath a sea or river.
explanation.definitionFit: The seabed or riverbed is the lowest part of the water, its base or underside.

clue.text: Display is set in Heaven

indicators.note: something set in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: to parade something is to put it on show
taken as written

explanation.surface: An exhibition of artwork is staged in the afterlife.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradise is the religious name for the abode of the blessed, another word for the next world in glory.

clue.text: European country with one short bridge

indicators.note: short of something means lacking it, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: a country of southern Europe
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A European nation with a single little bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One short' looks like it describes the bridge, but the country is short of one, losing its I.
explanation.definitionFit: A span is the stretch between supports, and as a verb it means to cross over, as a bridge does.

clue.text: Is its output measured in degrees?

definitions.text: Is its output measured in degrees?

blocks.clueFragment: Is its output measured in degrees?
blocks.note: surface reading: something whose product is gauged by temperature or angle, such as a furnace

blocks.clueFragment: Is its output measured in degrees?
blocks.note: setter's reading: an institution whose graduates leave with BA and BSc qualifications

explanation.walkthrough: Degrees suggests heat or angles; here it means academic qualifications.
explanation.definitionFit: A university awards academic degrees, so the number of graduates is literally a count of degrees conferred.

clue.text: Letter to Times sure to be revealing

blocks.note: the letter X, spelt out, is the multiplication sign read as 'times'
certain, as in 'I'm positive'

explanation.surface: A correspondent writes to The Times newspaper confident that the letter will expose something.
explanation.walkthrough: The Times looks like the newspaper, but it is the times sign of arithmetic, whose letter is X, written as a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Expositive means setting out or explaining, so a revealing statement exposes or lays bare its subject.

clue.text: Most wealthy independent church to be still around

indicators.note: the stillness word is placed around the others, enclosing them

blocks.note: to rest is to keep still
I is the abbreviation for independent
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: The wealthiest free church is content to remain where it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Richest is the superlative of rich, meaning having the greatest wealth of all.

clue.text: Satisfy a couple of leading players wanting relaxation

blocks.note: taken as written
the leading letter of players, taken twice to make a couple
ease is rest and freedom from effort

explanation.surface: A pair of star performers demanding time off must be kept happy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading players' sounds like the stars of a cast, but it means the first letter of players, taken twice.
explanation.definitionFit: To appease someone is to pacify them by giving them what they want, which is to satisfy them.

clue.text: A slip you had to pay for?

definitions.text: A slip you had to pay for?

blocks.clueFragment: A slip you had to pay for?
blocks.note: surface reading: a mistake or a fall that cost you dearly

blocks.clueFragment: A slip you had to pay for?
blocks.note: setter's reading: a slip of paper handed over when a purchase is paid for

explanation.walkthrough: Slip suggests an error or a stumble; here it is a small piece of paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop gives a paper record of payment after a purchase, a slip that you effectively paid to get.

clue.text: Met Sherry's new collection of would-be poets

indicators.note: a new version of the letters means they are made up into something fresh

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone encountered a woman named Sherry and her latest gathering of amateur versifiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhymester is a writer of trivial or poor verse, someone who rhymes without being a true poet.

clue.text: Article in colour rejected as expensive

indicators.note: the article goes in, inside the colour word
something rejected is turned back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a colour
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A colourful item of clothing is turned down because it costs too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' looks like a garment or item, but it is the grammatical article a.
explanation.definitionFit: Dear is a British way of saying costly, as in 'petrol is dear'.

clue.text: Something containing many layers?

blocks.note: surface reading: an object with lots of strata, like a cake or rock
setter's reading: a building full of hens that lay eggs

explanation.walkthrough: Layers suggests strata; here a layer is a bird that lays.
explanation.definitionFit: Laying hens are called layers, and the shed where poultry are kept holds lots of them.

clue.text: A Parisian affair leads to ruin

blocks.note: the French for a
a do is a party or event

explanation.surface: A French love affair ends in disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affair' suggests romance, but it means an event, a do.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo someone is to bring about their downfall, as in 'pride was his undoing'.

clue.text: Backing group taking time to reveal their principles

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the whole thing is read in reverse
the group takes the time into itself, holding it inside

blocks.note: a set is a group
ten o'clock is a time

explanation.surface: A band of backing singers takes time to show what they stand for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing group' reads as backing singers, but 'Backing' turns round the group once it has taken in the hour.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenets are beliefs or doctrines held as true, the basic rules a person or group lives by.

clue.text: Gazed back at old Bob, looking angry

indicators.note: back says the following words are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: taken as written
a bob was a shilling in old British money, abbreviated s
red in the face with rage

explanation.surface: Someone glared back at a man called Bob, flushed with anger.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob is not a name: a bob was the old British shilling, written s.
explanation.definitionFit: To stare is to look fixedly for a long time, the same as to gaze.

clue.text: Players can pop in here for a change

definitions.text: Players can pop in here for a change

blocks.clueFragment: Players can pop in here for a change
blocks.note: surface reading: somewhere performers might visit for variety

blocks.clueFragment: Players can pop in here for a change
blocks.note: setter's reading: the building at a cricket ground where the team gets changed

explanation.walkthrough: 'For a change' sounds like 'for variety'; here it means to change clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: At a cricket ground the clubhouse building where players change and watch play is called the pavilion.
